overview: Archaeopteryx lithographica is the iconic transitional form between non-avian dinosaurs and modern birds, from the Late Jurassic Solnhofen Limestone of Bavaria (~150 Ma). Its exquisite feather impressions — preserved in the fine-grained limestone — show pennaceous flight feathers identical in structure to those of modern birds on a skeleton that retains numerous non-avian features: teeth, a long bony tail and free clawed fingers.

Twelve specimens are currently recognised, the first found just two years after Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859. The timing was extraordinary: Archaeopteryx became the central exhibit in debates about evolution, gradualism and the relationship between reptiles and birds. It remains one of the most studied and argued-over fossils in history.

fossilSites.name: Solnhofen Limestone — Altmühl Valley
fossilSites.note: Tithonian lagoonal limestone yielding twelve Archaeopteryx specimens; the Berlin specimen (Humboldt Museum) and London specimen (NHM) are the most complete.

fossilSites.name: Mörnsheim Formation
fossilSites.note: Slightly younger and deeper-water limestone with one additional Archaeopteryx specimen (Bürgermeister-Müller specimen).

articles.title: Discovery and scientific impact
articles.body: The isolated Archaeopteryx feather was described in 1861; the first skeleton (now in London) was described the same year by Richard Owen. The Berlin specimen — found in 1877 and described in 1884 — is the most complete and widely displayed. Huxley used Archaeopteryx alongside Compsognathus to argue that birds descended from dinosaurs in the 1860s; this was later challenged and only definitively confirmed by cladistic analyses in the 1980s–90s.

articles.title: Mosaic of ancestral and derived features
articles.body: Non-avian (dinosaurian) features include: teeth in both jaws, three free clawed fingers on the wing, a long bony tail with vertebrae, gastralia (belly ribs) and a pubis pointing forward-and-downward. Avian features include: large pennaceous flight feathers, a wishbone (furcula), a reversed hallux (back toe), and a brain shape convergent with modern birds. This combination is the textbook definition of a transitional fossil.

articles.title: Flight capability
articles.body: Whether Archaeopteryx could fly actively, glide from trees, or was primarily a ground-dwelling runner with aerodynamic arms is debated. Bone density studies and flight-muscle attachment scar analysis suggest some aerial capability, but the lack of a keeled sternum indicates less powerful flight muscle attachment than in modern birds. It was probably a capable glider and possibly a flap-assisted runner, occupying an early position on the bird flight spectrum.

fossilRecord.formations: Solnhofen Limestone and related Late Jurassic lithographic limestones (e.g. Mörnsheim and Painten formations), Bavaria, Germany
fossilRecord.material: About 13–14 specimens preserving feather impressions, skeletal detail and sometimes soft-tissue outlines.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Jurassic shallow tropical lagoon environment in what is now Bavaria.
fossilRecord.evidence: Feather impressions on arms and tail alongside teeth, clawed fingers and bony tail confirm transitional status between dinosaurs and birds.

record.description: Archaeopteryx was a feathered early avialan from the Solnhofen Archipelago limestones of Germany. More than a dozen skeletal specimens, many with flight-feather impressions, document a mosaic of avian and non-avian theropod features.
facts: Asymmetrical wing feathers support aerodynamic function, while flight style remains debated.
The number and limits of Archaeopteryx species are contested; not every specimen is necessarily conspecific.
record.locomotion: bipedal; capable of active flight, exact flight style debated

presentation.heroLead: A crow-sized feathered theropod from the Solnhofen lagoons of Germany, long treated as the earliest bird and still the classic fossil of the dinosaur–bird transition.

heroMedia.title: Life restoration of Archaeopteryx lithographica
heroMedia.alt: Life restoration of a feathered Archaeopteryx running with wings spread in pursuit of a small theropod at night
heroMedia.caption: A restoration showing Archaeopteryx with the asymmetrical wing feathers and long feathered tail preserved in the fossils. The nocturnal setting, the prey and colour are interpretive; melanosome evidence suggests at least some black feathers.

animalParagraphs: Archaeopteryx was a small feathered theropod about half a metre long from snout to tail-tip, roughly the size of a raven, with a mass estimated at under a kilogram. It combined bird-like features, including a wishbone, a partly reversed first toe and true flight feathers, with ancestral traits such as toothed jaws, three clawed fingers and a long bony tail.

The animals lived on islands in a shallow tropical sea, and their carcasses sank into fine lime mud that preserved feather impressions in exquisite detail. The wing feathers are asymmetrical, as in flying birds, and the bone walls of the wing are proportioned like those of birds that flap in short bursts, supporting some capacity for powered flight even though the shoulder lacks a modern bird's arrangement.

Its teeth and claws suggest a diet of insects and small vertebrates, but no gut contents are known. Feathers preserved on the body, legs and tail are directly observed; the colour of the animal rests on a single isolated feather whose melanosomes suggest black, and that feather's assignment to Archaeopteryx is itself uncertain.
animalHighlights: Asymmetrical flight feathers and a long feathered tail are preserved directly on several skeletons.
Toothed jaws, clawed hands and a long bony tail mark it as a theropod dinosaur as well as an early avialan.
Around a dozen skeletons from one region make it one of the best-documented small Jurassic theropods.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Small pointed teeth and grasping hands point to insects and small animals; no stomach contents have been found.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Feather shape and wing-bone geometry support some powered flight, but the shoulder and breastbone differ from modern birds so its flight style is contested.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Several articulated specimens give lengths directly; individuals differ in size, and some may be immature.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Wing, tail and leg feathers are preserved as impressions; overall colouring is unknown apart from evidence for black in one feather.

whereFacts.label: Type locality
whereFacts.value: Langenaltheim quarry district near Solnhofen, Bavaria

locality.name: Solnhofen lithographic limestones
locality.note: Specimens come from several quarries around Solnhofen, Eichstätt and Schamhaupten. The lagoon deposits also yield Compsognathus, pterosaurs and many marine animals.

presentation.classificationSummary: Archaeopteryx is an early member of Avialae, the branch of maniraptoran theropods that includes birds. Its exact position relative to Anchiornis-like paravians and later birds has shifted between analyses, and the number of valid species within the genus remains debated.

related.reason: A small non-avialan theropod from the same Solnhofen deposits, useful for comparison.
Compare with a slightly older feathered paravian from China with similar wing and leg plumage.
Compare with a later toothless Early Cretaceous bird that shows the next steps in avian evolution.

questions.title: How many species are there?
questions.copy: A. lithographica and A. siemensii are widely accepted, but some specimens have been placed in separate genera and the boundaries between species are contested.

questions.title: Could it really fly?
questions.copy: Feather asymmetry and wing-bone geometry support flapping flight over short distances, yet the flight stroke of a modern bird was probably not possible.

questions.title: What colour was it?
questions.copy: Melanosome evidence suggests black in one isolated feather, but that feather may not belong to Archaeopteryx and the rest of the plumage is unknown.

review.ageReviewNote: The principal Solnhofen and Altmuehltal specimens are late Kimmeridgian to early Tithonian.

specimens.name: Holotype (London specimen)
specimens.note: Largely complete skeleton with feather impressions found in 1861; fixed as the name-bearing type of A. lithographica by the ICZN in 2011.

specimens.name: Berlin specimen
specimens.note: The most complete specimen, with skull, wings and tail feathers preserved; type of A. siemensii.

panel.headline: About a dozen slab skeletons, several nearly complete with feathers.
panel.standfirst: Archaeopteryx is known from roughly a dozen skeletal specimens and an isolated feather, all from the Late Jurassic lithographic limestones of Bavaria. The London and Berlin specimens alone preserve almost the whole skeleton with wing and tail plumage.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every skeletal region is known from multiple articulated individuals, several with feather impressions, though most are crushed flat on slabs and skull detail depends on a few specimens.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Articulated skeletons with skulls, vertebral columns, long bony tails, wishbones, wings with three clawed fingers, pelves and hindlimbs, plus impressions of wing, tail and leg feathers on several specimens. An isolated feather found in 1861 is of uncertain attribution.
knownRemains.note: The fossils are preserved as flattened impressions in fine limestone, so three-dimensional skull anatomy and braincase detail rely on a few specimens and CT scanning.

media.title: The Berlin specimen, MB.Av.101
media.alt: The Berlin specimen of Archaeopteryx on its limestone slab, showing the skull, spread wings with feather impressions and long feathered tail
media.caption: The original Berlin specimen at the Museum für Naturkunde, discovered around 1874–75 and the most complete Archaeopteryx skeleton, with clear wing and tail feather impressions.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Several skulls with toothed jaws, mostly crushed; braincase and inner ear studied by CT in the London specimen.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Complete neck, back and sacrum, and the long bony tail of about twenty vertebrae, in several articulated specimens.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Furcula, shoulder girdle, wings with three clawed fingers, pelvis and hindlimbs with a partly reversed first toe.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Impressions of asymmetrical wing feathers, tail feathers and leg plumage on several specimens; melanosomes reported from an isolated feather.

specimenCards.title: NHMUK PV OR 37001 · London specimen
specimenCards.description: A largely complete skeleton with feather impressions, found in 1861 near Langenaltheim, purchased by the British Museum and described by Richard Owen in 1863. It was formally fixed as the name-bearing type of A. lithographica in 2011.
specimenCards.meta: Langenaltheim, Bavaria · Solnhofen Limestone · Natural History Museum, London

specimenCards.title: MB.Av.101 · Berlin specimen
specimenCards.description: Discovered in the Blumenberg quarry near Eichstätt and acquired by the Berlin museum in 1880. It preserves the skull, wings and tail with feathers in place and is the basis for most reconstructions.
specimenCards.meta: Eichstätt, Bavaria · Solnhofen Limestone · Museum für Naturkunde, Berlin

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Around a dozen articulated skeletons with toothed skulls, clawed wings, long bony tails and impressions of flight and body feathers.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: An early avialan capable of at least short bursts of flapping flight, combining bird and non-avian theropod features; species divisions rest on subtle skeletal differences.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Overall plumage colour, flight performance and ecology, diet, and whether all specimens belong to one or several species.
